speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He goes on to ask whether the private housing land use comparables that are used to value land for HDB BTO flats are based on records of the last transacted private residential land sold by the Government and private parties.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The land sold to the private sector for private housing development is typically done by open tender through the Government Land Sales, or GLS, programme.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The value of the land is determined through price discovery as developers bid for the land.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: On the other hand, sale of state land to HDB for public housing developments does not fall under GLS.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Instead, the Chief Valuer considers relevant public housing transactions and the specific parameters of the site.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is in part because of the greater restrictions that apply to public housing such as buyers' citizenship status, minimum occupation period, income ceiling, non-ownership of private properties and so on.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I must caveat that I am saying this broadly at the expense of technical accuracy and detail of the work actually done by the Chief Valuer, which is an independent office.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But suffice to say, he adopts the same valuation principles used by professional valuers in the private sector and these principles are also consistent with the principles that other valuers use to value public housing or HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, when your residents apply for loans, they get the valuation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is what the valuer does – determine the value of HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There is such a thing as the value of public housing and public housing land and it can be ascertained.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He argues that by doing so, HDB flats can be made even cheaper than they are.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I will leave the point about HDB home pricing and affordability for the debate that we will all be having soon.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But we will deal with the point about valuation of land for public housing today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Professional valuers in the private sector will tell us that.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And actually, all of us intrinsically understand this.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, when Mr Leong calls for land to be sold at historical cost, he is overturning this fundamental point that land has value.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Given that most Singaporeans own their homes, he is essentially saying that by a stroke of his pen, a significant portion of the asset value should be ignored.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, this was the discussion too that Mr Chiam See Tong had with then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew back on 21 March 1985 in Parliament, where Mr Chiam was arguing about what the real value of HDB land was and whether it could really be discovered.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And after some to-ing and fro-ing, if you check Hansard, then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew stood up and asked the Member squarely.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Lee asked, "May I ask whether the Member concedes that there is such a concept called 'value of land'?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And that there is such a profession known in Singapore as a Land Valuer?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That the Government has a Chief Land Valuer?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That there are, in the private sector, experts who regularly go to Court and give evidence as to what the value of land is?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And that the Ministry of National Development, by transferring it from the HDB to the Government, is in fact making the books widely known that the value of each plot of land will be determined, and is determinable, because the land can be used for defence, it can be used for schools, it can be used for condominiums, it can be used for HDB, it can be used for URA, who is prepared to pay what price for what use.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Is there no such concept as value of land?" That in a way is a rhetorical question that he asked at the end.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And after some further exchanges, Mr Chiam accepted that if that was what the Prime Minister said, then that was what he said.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Perhaps grudgingly but I think that made the point clear.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, when you buy and sell land or property in Singapore, and I will say in many parts of the world, you may often call for a valuation report.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The valuer will usually apply established and accepted valuation principles accepted by the profession and by the public to determine current market value.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, he looks at the relevant recent transactions, makes adjustments for attributes and so on, and produces the valuation report, detailing his grounds.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But I do not think you or your professional valuer will base your transaction on how much the property had changed hands back in history.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Third, the idea of valuing land at historical cost sounds attractive but is really problematic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If the land was acquired by the Government in the 1960s, HDB pays for the land at 1960s' pricing?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If the land was, say, recently acquired, maybe 2015, then HDB pays the 2015 price, far higher than before?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And what if the land had all along been state land and was never acquired by anyone or from anyone?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Is the value of the state land at historical cost then zero, that is, HDB pays zero dollars?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Or do we go back to 1819 or thereabouts or further back in time to try to find some historical transactional record that was made and say, "Ah, that is the price"?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I think most people will understand why this is wrong.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If you want to sell your property today, whether it is an HDB flat, condo, terrace house, shophouse or office, you will look at what it is worth in the market today and use that as some basis for you to transact, to bargain or to negotiate.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Imagine if someone comes up to you and says point blank, "Hey, he should really be paying you the historical cost instead of market price", that is, how much you or your forefathers had paid for it way back in the past – let us use that as the basis, as it is really what it costs to you or your lineage.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Or imagine one of our Pioneer Generation Singaporeans, one of our seniors, maybe in the past earning $500 a month, maybe more, maybe less; and who may have paid say $50,000 for his flat back in the early days.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, because Singapore has done well thanks to his generation's hard work and contribution, it is certainly worth a lot more.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When you go and do house visits, many seniors tell you proudly they are still living in the flat but it is worth a lot more.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If you adopt Mr Leong's new approach, would this senior be required to sell at just above $50,000 or even with say, COV, cash over historical value?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Would his children and descendants inherit a flat valued as it was back then in the 1960s, that is, worth very little compared to today's prices?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We know that Mr Leong makes a superficially attractive proposition but we know that the proposal is unfair; it is not logical and simply cannot fly in the face of long-established, well-accepted valuation principles.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Fourth, Mr Leong's valuation approach is actually dangerous for Singapore, because it is not really about valuation principles at all.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As my colleague Minister Ms Indranee Rajah had explained late last year, state land is part of our national reserves – quite different from other countries, other provinces, other cities, other districts in other countries which use the sale of state land as a way to fund their recurrent expenditure.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Its value grows if Singapore is well-managed and does well.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If our reserves are well-husbanded and grow, they give greater assurance that our future generations of Singaporeans will have resources to deal with crises, catastrophe and calamity, like pandemics, like war, like economic crises, like climate emergencies.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If they grow, they not just benefit the security of our future generations, but they also benefit us today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And FMV is determined by professional valuation principles.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When Mr Leong advances his argument, it is about affordable housing, cheap housing; it is about valuation approach.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, it is complicated, with lots of charts, but the end product is housing will be a lot cheaper, but hey presto, with no need to pay more today by you.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He says everything else but through sleight of hand, he hides from you the plain fact that he is really wanting to raid our reserves.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We spend considerable amounts of national resources to keep our BTO flats affordable: at the house price-to-income ratios being comparable to other countries, where you can see the stark difference; at the mortgage servicing ratios as they are.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Leong says he can make them even cheaper.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But to do this, there is one way: cut back on other Government expenditure, whether it is healthcare, security, education, or whatever you would want to trim back so that you spend more on this.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Or by raising revenues through taxation or through other means, so that he can deliver on even cheaper BTO flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But they are not going to be popular or wearable.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Get the benefit of the cake and eat it.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had said previously in a debate on the GST and on many other occasions, if you want to tap more on the reserves, diminish it, use more of it for today and leave less for tomorrow, let us just say it plainly – let Singaporeans see it as it is and we can have a debate come the next round when we talk about housing, about reserves, about expenditure, about sustainability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the high resale prices that we have seen in recent years push up the value of BTO flats and impact the price that Singaporeans pay for their BTO flats?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Or does HDB increase subsidies to completely offset the increase in land valuation due to this factor?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, the Chief Valuer's decision on the valuation of a piece of land has a great impact on the amounts that Singaporeans have to pay for their HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government ensure that, in practice, the Chief Valuer is able to make his valuation decisions completely independently and that no one attempts to influence his decisions?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is in the Constitution his powers and his protection are set out in law.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is presidential protection on the Office of the Chief Valuer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member may be thinking about what the private sector does.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The private sector developer bids for a piece of land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It has to be very careful how much it bids for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It then says, "Okay, let me call my consultant and contractor to ask about the costs of development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And then, let me set my per-square-foot price or price my units in order to recover my costs and also to make a profit." That must be it – being a profit-driven private sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I have said – and my colleagues and my predecessors have said – we do not price HDB flats to recover cost of land and construction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in some time in our history, including in the last two years, these prices fluctuated a lot – material prices, labour cost and land cost have gone up quite a bit because of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If it were so, then, would you not see BTO prices shooting up?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we do not price HDB flats to recover costs of land and construction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is why HDB collects far less than the costs it has to pay out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And the deficit has been growing, especially the last two years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is first and foremost, the fallacy in the Member's question; and I hope that by this explanation, you understand how it is done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I go to the Member's first question where you asked how we ensure that resale price increases in the last two years do not overly push up BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think what I have just explained answers that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In order to keep the price of BTO flats relatively steady, despite all these resale price increases, we first look at transactions of resale flats that are comparable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We can have further debate on this when the PSP and the Government debate this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We welcome the WP to participate as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just following up from Minister's point on subsidies – I filed a written question for yesterday's session, enquiring the dollar value of subsidies allocated by HDB in each year from 2010 to 2022 for HDB BTO apartments in both mature and non-mature estates respectively, and how many of such flats were constructed each year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister replied saying that the market subsidies are not directly comparable across projects, launches and years as they depend on prevailing market conditions, attributes of the BTO projects offered and prevailing household incomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But Minister in his reply did not set out the subsidies for each year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I cannot understand why that information cannot be made public because those subsidies are taxpayers' subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The taxpayer is actually funding the home ownership programme, vis a vis subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I need the Minister's explanation as to why that information cannot be given out by the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think we can deal with this more thoroughly in a debate on a Motion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The short answer is if you look at every brochure when we have a launch – and I am sure the Member has got residents come up to him to say, "Which one, 3-room, 4-room, which floor" – and if you look at the range of BTO prices, we made the effort to put the comparable resale price next to it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is a sense, broadly, of the whole range of market subsidies that are given to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we have to bear in mind that based on each family's circumstances, additional grants may or may not be available.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, it will vary, not just project by project, but also depending on who buys it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, not just subsidies but also grants that a flat buyer receives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we have provided the cost of construction, which is put out and published.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we also put it in the brochure, not just for Members of Parliament but for individual buyers to get a sense of the range of the difference between the resale prices that are comparable and the prices that they are being asked to pay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Again, prices come in a range due to different floor, different facing, different block.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And of course, as I have said before, the subsidies that we provide, on top of the grants, will vary from launch to launch, from year to year, even within the same town, because and especially when resale prices fluctuate a lot.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I mean, when the market is flat, the subsidy is roughly about the same.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But just think about it: you have resale prices shooting up 28%, 29% in the last two years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I may be getting my figures a bit wrong but broadly, you know the resale price has gone up a lot.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They have remained relatively stable – of course, adjusting for different locations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That must mean that you have to adjust the subsidies even for projects launched in succession in an area, in order to ensure that there is stability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we talk about valuation and its impact on BTO prices, as we know, because of the current situation of supply, the affordability of resale flats is also in question.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how can we assure people if BTO is not an option and they are going into the resale market, that it is still affordable, especially for first-time home owners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We all recognise that resale prices have gone up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also mindful of the headwinds that may come our way this year – economic headwinds, geopolitical headwinds, very high mortgage interest rates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, all in, let us keep an eye on the resale market, both private and HDB.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: People are being rather prudent and careful as they should be.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are macro prudential rules to constrain overstretching.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister one question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure when I mentioned that HDB prices should be priced based on historical cost of land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There was an exchange between the hon Member and Senior Minister of State Sim Ann last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think we leave that for the debate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the Member tells us that he does not think Government should charge HDB at historical prices, then I think that advances the discussion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Orders of the day.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
